items.reason: The strategy shuts down the factory-owned pool, so strategies created after rebalance reuse dead queues and acknowledge unprocessed messages.

This lock-creation race claim matches no golden issue. The implementation returns dict.setdefault's stored lock, so concurrent callers constructing candidate locks does not establish that they receive different locks.
Setting the worker shutdown flag causes workers to exit before draining queued work, which is the golden shutdown problem.
Unbounded queues and unconditional acceptance provide no backpressure, allowing backlog memory to grow without limit.

This alleges commit-scan CPU overhead, distinct from the golden issues about commit correctness across offset gaps. Its sparse-range claim is also inaccurate: the loop breaks at the first missing or outstanding offset, although min/max still scan the stored set.
The group-concurrency test checks completion counts and group presence without verifying overlapping processing, so serial execution passes.
The subscription-concurrency test only checks processor call count, so it cannot detect a regression to serial execution.
The worker completes offsets after processing exceptions, allowing failed messages to be committed despite the successful-processing guarantee.
The advertised backpressure does not exist because worker queues are unbounded and submissions are accepted unconditionally.
Unconditional offset completion in finally makes failed processing committable and silently skips failed results.
FilteredPayload reaches a decoder that explicitly rejects it, causing exception logging and fallback handling instead of the intended skip path. No golden issue describes this decoder mismatch.
